Q01: Canonicalize endpoints with least/greatest, then retain row_number = 1 ordered by row_id within (lo, hi, dist). dropDuplicates on the canonical keys alone cannot promise the smallest original row_id. The left-join alternative explicitly tests that no earlier equivalent row exists; a left_anti join with the same condition is another direct expression. Ranking is usually preferable to generating all earlier matches for a heavily duplicated route.
Q02: Alias both inputs and require different physical IDs before distinct removes repeated output pairs. That identity check makes one self-pair insufficient. Deduplicating the input first would erase the evidence that two identical self-pair rows exist. The self join can expand greatly for frequent pairs.
Q03: Create both directions, remove self edges, and distinct the (person, neighbor) pairs. A left join from the people master keeps isolates; count(neighbor) ignores the null placeholder produced by that join. count(*) would incorrectly give an isolate one neighbor.
Q04: Normalize each undirected edge so a < b. Join a-b to b-c, then use a left_semi join to require the closing a-c edge without adding columns or multiplying matching paths. The strict ordering yields one representation of each triangle; high-degree vertices can still create many candidate paths.
Q05: Seed every node as its own root, follow edges in both directions, and retain only previously unseen (root, node) pairs at each iteration. MIN(root) gives the component label and isolates survive their seeds. See the reachability helper for cycle termination and checkpoint setup. The all-pairs closure can grow quadratically within a large component; a graph library or minimum-label propagation is a better production starting point.
Q06: Deduplicate before assigning row_number. Subtracting the row position from each consecutive integer gives a constant island key. Grouping that key yields the endpoints and distinct length. The global ordered window is intentional for this single sequence; separate sequences need a business partition key.
Q07: Deduplicate (user_id, day_no), build each user's islands, then compare every streak length with that user's maximum. Equality retains all tied longest streaks. Ranking one streak first and taking row_number = 1 would discard ties.
Q08: Pad the observed IDs with 0 and 13, then use lead to find distances greater than one. The output endpoints are current + 1 and next - 1. This also handles an empty input without expanding all missing integers. The constants encode the question's inclusive 1–12 domain.
Q09: lag finds the preceding event within each user in (minute_no, event_id) order. Mark a boundary only for a gap greater than 30, and cumulatively sum boundary flags using an explicit ROWS frame. Equal timestamps and exactly 30-minute gaps stay in the same session.
Q10: A row continues a run only when the day is consecutive and status.eqNullSafe(previous_status) is true. The missing predecessor starts a new run, including when the first status is null. A cumulative boundary count separates recurring statuses and missing-day breaks.
Q11: Filter attendance before computing id minus row_number, because a low-attendance row must interrupt the qualifying ID sequence. Count each island with a partition window, then preserve all original rows from islands of size at least three. The date column does not define adjacency here.
Q12: For these non-overlapping one-day tasks, start_day minus row_number is constant across adjoining tasks. Aggregate the smallest start and greatest end; subtract them for the half-open project duration. Variable-length or overlapping tasks require interval packing instead.
Q13: The shared pack_intervals helper compares each start with the maximum end of ALL preceding rows. Using lag(end_at) fails for nested intervals whose immediately preceding end is short. Strictly greater starts split islands, so touching ranges merge. Ordering also includes the unique ID.
Q14: Pack occupied intervals first, append zero-length boundary markers at 0 and 20, then take gaps from an end to the next start. The markers preserve leading/trailing space and yield the entire window when there are no bookings. The input contract already confines bookings to the requested window.
Q15: Union +1 start and -1 end events, and sum deltas at each timestamp BEFORE computing the running occupancy. This implements half-open boundaries at tied times. lead supplies the segment end; retain every positive-duration segment tied at maximum occupancy. Adjacent peak segments are reported separately, matching the question.
Q16: Pack intervals with the same helper as Q13, sum their disjoint lengths, and coalesce the empty aggregate to zero. Summing original lengths double-counts overlap. This is a global occupied-time measure; per-resource occupancy must partition packing by resource.
Q17: Filter changes to the as-of date before ranking them newest first per product. Keep one eligible row and left join from the complete product master, filling absent prices with 10. The contract makes (product_id, day_no) unique; real revisions on the same day need an additional tie-break key.
Q18: Put key equality and both validity boundaries in the LEFT join condition. The start is inclusive; the end is exclusive or open when null. Filtering the joined result on validity would drop uncovered facts. Overlapping dimension periods would multiply fact rows and violate the declared contract.
Q19: Build target/reading candidates and rank by absolute distance, reading time, then reading ID. This is an exact, readable reference but generates targets × readings candidates. Large datasets need a carefully validated nearest-neighbor/range strategy; a fixed time band alone can incorrectly miss the actual nearest reading.
Q20: A left_anti join returns customers for which no equality match exists. A null purchase customer_id does not match a registered ID and cannot poison the whole result as NOT IN can. Duplicate matching purchases do not duplicate the preserved customers.
Q21: Filter to paid orders and aggregate them by customer before joining to the customer master. Fill the missing count with zero. A post-join status filter would remove customers with only cancelled orders or no orders.
Q22: Aggregate orders and payments separately to one row per customer, then join those totals to the master. This restores a common grain before joining the two independent child tables. sumDistinct(amount) is not a valid repair for fan-out because equal transaction amounts are legitimate.
Q23: Use a left_semi join against approved tags to preserve each eligible invoice exactly once. Sum the original invoice amounts, keeping identical amounts on distinct invoices. Coalesce the empty aggregate to zero. A regular join can multiply invoices when approved tags repeat.
Q24: A full outer join exposes additions and removals. Test row presence using the non-null ID, and use eqNullSafe on the values so null-to-null is unchanged while null-to-value changes are visible. Coalesce the two ID columns only for the output identifier, not for detecting row presence.
Q25: Assign -1 to every old occurrence and +1 to every new occurrence, union without deduplication, then sum by key. Spark groups null keys together, so their multiplicity is reconciled too. Explicit nulls-first sorting matches the expected output. except/subtract would erase duplicate counts.
Q26: Form required customer/product pairs, anti join purchased pairs to find missing requirements, then anti join those customers from the master. An empty required set produces no missing pairs and therefore retains everybody. The Cartesian requirement grid is clear for study but can be large; a coverage-count plan can avoid materializing it when its empty-set semantics are preserved.
Q27: Start with Q26's complete coverage, then reject anyone with a purchase outside the required set. Coverage alone allows extras and is insufficient for equality. Empty requirements leave only customers with empty baskets. Both stages use anti joins, so purchase duplicates cannot change qualification.
Q28: Aggregate each non-null product set with collect_set, sort the array into a deterministic canonical representation, and fill missing baskets with a typed empty array. Equality of these arrays means exact set equality, including empty baskets. Array state must fit per customer; for huge baskets, compare relational differences instead. A hash-only comparison would need collision handling.
Q29: Compute minimum and maximum scores per exam, semi join students who participated, and anti join everyone tied at either extreme. Equal extreme scores exclude every tied student. The participation semi join separately excludes students who took no exams.
Q30: Compute two window counts at their independent grains: prior_value and (lat, lon). Apply both predicates only after both counts are computed over all policies. Filtering on one condition first would change the population used by the other count.
Q31: Use ROWS with (at, id) for a deterministic row-by-row total. Use RANGE ordered only by at for timestamp peers. Adding id to the RANGE ordering would split timestamp peers and change the requested result. Final output is explicitly sorted because a DataFrame has no inherent row order.
Q32: The window spans the complete user partition, from unbounded preceding through unbounded following. last with ignorenulls=False preserves a null final value. A prefix frame would return the last value so far. An unordered groupBy().agg(last(...)) does not implement this deterministic ordered requirement.
Q33: last with ignorenulls=True over the ordered prefix directly expresses forward fill. Leading nulls have no previous non-null value and stay null. max is wrong when observed values decrease. Include the ID to define ordering for equal timestamps.
Q34: Generate the five report days, aggregate sales per day, left join, and fill missing revenue with zero. Only then does a three-row window mean three calendar days. Compute the window before filtering incomplete initial report days, and use fractional division before rounding.
Q35: Join each report day to activity in its inclusive three-day range, then count distinct users. The left join preserves zero-activity report days. Adding daily distinct counts would double-count a user active on multiple days. This range join is a correctness reference whose expansion must be assessed for long reporting horizons.
Q36: Mark only each non-null user's first occurrence in event order, then prefix-sum those markers. Repeated users and null users contribute zero. This avoids a distinct window aggregate and preserves every event. The global event order is a potential single-partition bottleneck at production scale.
Q37: Assign positions with a salary-and-ID ordering while retaining duplicate salaries as distinct observations. Select floor((n+1)/2) through floor((n+2)/2), then average those central observations. Spark division does not reproduce SQLite integer truncation automatically, so the floors are explicit. This is exact, not an approximate quantile.
Q38: Convert frequencies into cumulative rank intervals, then join exactly TWO middle positions to their containing intervals. Do not distinct the positions: an odd-size population intentionally supplies the same central position twice. The algorithm never expands frequency observations. Integer DIV and remainder preserve central positions even above the exact-integer range of a double. Total frequency must still fit LongType; larger populations need explicit decimal arithmetic.
Q39: A ROWS prefix sum ordered by unique turn determines eligibility. Positive weights make the total monotone, so the greatest eligible turn is exactly the final admitted person. Zero or negative weights would require a different first-failure treatment. limit(1) returns no row when the first person cannot fit.
Q40: Prefix-sum reset flags into a segment ID, then prefix-sum amounts within that segment. The reset row belongs to the new segment and has zero amount, giving zero displayed total. Negative amounts are retained and do not imply another reset.
Q41: lead looks at the next two ROW POSITIONS in sequence order, independent of gaps in seq values. A run of three or more contains at least one matching three-row window. Ordinary equality excludes nulls under this question's contract, and distinct returns each qualifying value once.
Q42: Use row_number to establish alternating pair positions rather than parity of sparse seat IDs. Odd positions take the next occupant, even positions take the previous occupant. An odd final row has no next occupant and retains its own, which is non-null by contract.
Q43: Union both player roles into a single (player, score) stream using union, which preserves all match contributions. Aggregate scores and left join registered players, filling missing totals with zero. Rank within group by descending score and ascending ID to make the tie-break deterministic.
Q44: Deduplicate (user_id, day_no) activity before joining the exact signup_day + 1 condition. The left join leaves exactly one row per registered user, so averaging the 0/1 return flag uses the fixed signup denominator. Counting raw activity would overweight users with repeated events.
Q45: Sum credits per account/month before comparing with the account limit. Filter strictly over-limit months, then use lag to require the preceding over-limit month to be exactly current - 1. Month ordinals preserve December-to-January adjacency, and missing months break the condition.
Q46: Seed manager 1, expand only new reachable nodes, and exclude the seed in the final projection. The shared anti-join frontier helper terminates despite cycles and repeated edges. Checkpoint storage must remain accessible until the result is consumed. This uses directed edges, unlike Q05.
Q47: Build the distinct set of IDs that appear as parents, then left join a child-presence marker. Test parent_id is null FIRST so an isolated root stays Root. A distinct parent set avoids multiplying a node once per child.
Q48: Find the earliest view, then the earliest add strictly after that view, then any later buy. Choosing the earliest feasible prefix leaves the most room for later stages, so it cannot discard a valid sequence. Taking the earliest add without first requiring it to follow a view would miss valid later attempts. Additional constraints such as a maximum funnel duration need new logic.
Q49: Prefix quantities turn supplies and demands into intervals on one cumulative quantity axis. Their positive overlap length is allocated quantity. Strict hi > lo excludes zero-sized boundary matches. A general non-equi join can be expensive; this expresses FIFO correctness without collecting inventory to Python or iterating over units.
Q50: Compute cumulative receipts per product and total units sold. Each receipt keeps max(0, min(batch quantity, cumulative receipt end - sold)); multiply that remainder by its own cost. Fully consumed products still produce zero totals. The no-negative-stock and no-returns contracts justify valuing the final receipt suffix this way. Real currency should use an explicit DecimalType with an overflow policy.
